narratorIntro: Now turn to Part one. You will hear a man enquiring about membership at a community sports centre. First, you have some time to look at questions one to ten.
narratorOutro: That is the end of Part one.
body: — Riverbank Leisure Centre, good morning. Erin speaking.
— Oh, hello. I'd like to ask about joining, please. I've just moved into the area.
— Of course. I'll take a few details and then talk you through what we offer. Can I start with your surname?
— It's Whitfield.
— Could you spell that for me?
— Yes — W, H, I, T, F, I, E, L, D. Whitfield.
— Thank you. And a contact number?
— It's oh-seven-double-four, one-nine-six, three-eight-two. Sorry, that's my old one. Let me give you the new one — oh-seven-double-four, one-nine-six, three-two-eight.

— Three-two-eight at the end. Got it. Now, we run three kinds of membership. There's Standard, which is the gym and the pool. There's Active, which adds every class on the timetable. And there's Family, which covers two adults and up to three children.
— It would just be me. But I'd want the classes — I'm trying to get back into swimming properly, and there's a technique session I saw on your website.
— Then Active is the one you want. Standard wouldn't include that session.
— Active, then.
— Lovely. Active is normally fifty-two pounds a month. There's an introductory rate for the first three months, though, which brings it down to forty-five.
— Forty-five. That's better than I expected.

— It goes up to the full fifty-two in month four, so do bear that in mind. Now, everyone joining does a short induction before their first visit — it's about forty minutes with one of the instructors.
— When are those?
— We run them Tuesdays and Thursdays. This week Tuesday's already full, I'm afraid, so the next one would be Thursday.
— Thursday's fine.
— And the times are ten in the morning or six in the evening.
— Six, please. I don't finish work until half past four.
— Six it is. Do come in something you can move in — you'll be shown the machines and you'll actually use a couple of them. And bring a towel; we don't provide those.
— A towel. Right.
— One more thing about the lockers. They take a one-pound coin, and you get it back when you return the key — but if you lose the key there's a charge of fifteen pounds for a replacement.
— Fifteen. I'll be careful with it.
— Most people are. Now, was there a particular class you wanted me to book you onto? The technique one you mentioned is called Stroke Clinic, and it fills up.
— Yes, please — Stroke Clinic.
— Stroke Clinic, Thursday evenings after your induction. And last thing, for our records: how did you hear about the centre?
— A colleague, actually. Someone at work swims here.
— A recommendation. That's what most people say. Right, Mr Whitfield, you're all set. See you Thursday at six.

narratorIntro: Now turn to Part two. You will hear a volunteer coordinator showing a new group around the Riverbank Community Garden. First, you have some time to look at questions eleven to twenty.
narratorOutro: That is the end of Part two.
body: Good morning, everyone, and thank you for giving up your Saturday. Before we put anyone to work, let me walk you round the plan so you know where things are — you'll be surprised how often people end up watering the wrong beds.

So. You've come in through the gate at the bottom left, and the main path runs straight up from there, then turns right along the middle of the site. Keep that shape in your head and you won't get lost.
The site is two rows of plots. The top row runs along the river; the bottom row is the one you walk past on your way in from the gate.

So, first, the tool store. That's on the bottom row, the very first plot you come to from the entrance. Everything is signed inside and there's a list on the door — please put things back where the list says, not where there's a gap.

The compost area is on the same bottom row, but right along at the other end. Not the last plot — the one before it, third along. People do get this wrong, so: third along the bottom, with the pond after it.
Up on the top row now, along the river. The fruit cages are the first plot up there, directly above the tool store. They're netted, so the door is stiff — lift it rather than pull it.

The polytunnel is the biggest structure we have. It's on the top row too, at the far end, the very last plot in that row. It gets the afternoon sun in that corner, which is the whole reason it went there rather than nearer the gate.

And finally the wildlife pond, which is the one I want everyone to be careful around. It is the very last plot on the bottom row, in the corner. There's no fence — that's deliberate, for the hedgehogs — so watch your step, particularly if you've brought children.
Right. A few practical things.

First, the question everyone asks: can you take produce home? Yes, but not on your first day, and not by the bagful. The rule is that anything harvested on a session day goes to the share table by the entrance, and whatever's left at four o'clock, volunteers may take. It isn't about trust; it's that a share table is how we keep the neighbours on our side.

Second, tools. The powered tools — the mower and the strimmer — are for trained volunteers only, and the training runs once a month. Hand tools, anyone can use. Please don't be the person who decides today is the day they learn to strim.

Third, wet weather. We do not cancel for rain. We cancel for high wind, because of the trees along the river, and you'll get a text by eight in the morning if a session is off. If you haven't had a text, assume we're on.

Fourth, and this one has caught people out: parking. The car park behind the centre is not ours. It belongs to the health centre and they do issue tickets at weekends. There's free parking on Mill Lane, two minutes' walk, and that is what we'd recommend.

And last of all — what we most need from new volunteers is not muscle, honestly. It's people who come back. One person here every other Saturday for a year is worth far more to this garden than twenty people once.

narratorIntro: Now turn to Part three. You will hear two students, Priya and Sam, discussing a project on urban transport with each other. First, you have some time to look at questions twenty-one to thirty.
narratorOutro: That is the end of Part three.
body: — Sam, have you got ten minutes? I want to divide the transport project up before Friday.
— Yeah, now's good. I've got the brief here. Six sections, and we present for twenty minutes between us.
— Right. So section one is the literature review, and I'd honestly rather do that on my own. I've already read most of it, and two people reading the same forty papers is how we waste a week.
— No argument. That's yours.
— Section two is the survey design. That one I think we have to do together — if I write the questions and you analyse the answers, we'll end up with data that doesn't answer anything.
— Agreed. We sit down and draft the questions in the same room. Both of us.
— Good. Section three, the cycling case study — that's Amsterdam and Copenhagen.
— I'll take that. I spent a term there and I've still got contacts at the transport office.
— Perfect, it's yours. Section four is the bus network modelling, and that's the one I'm nervous about, because it needs the software.
— Which neither of us has used properly.
— Which is why I'd rather one of us learns it well than both of us learn it badly. I'll take it. I've got a fortnight before it's due and I'd rather that be my problem.
— If you're sure. Shout if it goes wrong.
— Section five is the interviews with commuters.
— That's got to be both of us — you can't run a focus group on your own and take notes at the same time.
— That's a fair point. Both, then.
— And section six, the cost comparison.
— I'll do that one too. It's spreadsheets, and I'm faster at spreadsheets than you are.
— I'm not going to pretend otherwise.
— Right. Now — the part I actually wanted to talk about. Doctor Ellis said our research question was too broad.
— She did. Although what she actually said was that it was too broad for the time we have. That's not the same as it being a bad question.
— No, it isn't. So do we narrow it, or do we keep it and say clearly what we couldn't cover?
— I'd narrow it. A report that admits it couldn't cover half its own question reads as though we ran out of time — which we did, but we don't have to advertise it.
— See, I'd go the other way. I think naming the limits is what makes it look deliberate rather than rushed.
— Hmm. We could do both. Narrow the question, and then have a limitations section that says what a wider study would have asked.
— That I'll agree to.
— Now, the presentation. Twenty minutes for six sections is three minutes each, which is nothing.
— We don't present all six. We present the two case studies properly and summarise the rest in one slide.
— Doctor Ellis will ask about the modelling, though. She always asks about the method.
— Then we have a slide ready for it, but we don't lead with it. There's a difference between being ready for a question and spending eight of our twenty minutes on it.
— Fine. One more thing — the deadline. It says Friday the fourteenth on the handbook, but the portal says the sixteenth.
— The portal is the one that counts. But I'd work to the fourteenth anyway.
— Why?
— Because every time I've worked to the real deadline, something has gone wrong on the last day.

narratorIntro: Now turn to Part four. You will hear a lecturer talking about urban heat and how cities are responding to it. First, you have some time to look at questions thirty-one to forty.
narratorOutro: That is the end of Part four.
body: Good afternoon. Today I want to talk about a problem that is easy to measure, hard to see, and increasingly expensive: the fact that a city is warmer than the countryside around it. The phenomenon has a name — the urban heat island — and I want to cover three things. What causes it, what it costs, and what actually works.

Let's begin with the cause, because there is a common misunderstanding here. People assume the heat is produced by the city: by cars, by air conditioning, by industry. Some of it is, but that is the smaller part. The larger part is not produced at all. It is stored.

Concrete, brick and asphalt have a high thermal mass. They absorb solar radiation through the day and release it slowly through the night. A field cools quickly after sunset; a street does not. And so the difference between a city and its surroundings is at its greatest not at noon, as you might expect, but a few hours after dark. In a large European city that night-time difference typically reaches four degrees, and in extreme conditions it has been measured above seven.

The second contributor is the absence of water. In a landscape with vegetation, a large share of incoming energy goes into evaporating water from leaves and soil — a process called evapotranspiration — and energy spent evaporating water is energy not spent raising the temperature. Pave that landscape and the water runs off into a drain within minutes. The cooling mechanism has been removed, and nothing replaced it.

The third is geometry. Narrow streets between tall buildings behave like a series of traps: radiation bounces between the walls rather than escaping upwards. Researchers describe this using the sky view factor — essentially, how much of the sky you can see from street level. The less sky, the less heat escapes.
So much for the cause. Now the cost.

The obvious cost is health, and it falls unevenly. During the 2003 heatwave in western Europe, mortality rose most sharply among people over seventy-five living alone on upper floors of buildings without ventilation. Heat is not distributed evenly across a city, and neither is the ability to escape it. The neighbourhoods that are hottest are, with tedious reliability, the neighbourhoods with the least tree cover, and those are rarely the wealthy ones.

The less obvious cost is energy. Air conditioning is a feedback loop: it cools a building by moving heat outside, which warms the street, which raises the demand for air conditioning. In dense districts this can raise the outdoor temperature by a further degree overnight.
Which brings me to what works, and here I want to be careful, because this field has a weakness for the photogenic solution.

The most effective intervention, by a wide margin, is trees — mature trees, in streets, in enough numbers to form a continuous canopy. Shade prevents the surface from absorbing the heat in the first place, which is worth more than removing it afterwards, and the evapotranspiration adds cooling on top. Measurements of well-shaded streets consistently show surface temperatures around ten degrees below unshaded ones nearby.

Second: surface colour. Painting roofs white, or using reflective paving, raises what is called the albedo — the proportion of sunlight reflected rather than absorbed. It is cheap, it works, and it is unglamorous.

Third, and this is the one I would ask you to be sceptical about: green roofs. They are popular with planners and they photograph beautifully. They do cool the building beneath them, and they help with rainfall. But a green roof five storeys up does very little for the temperature of the street below, and the street is where people actually are. It is not that they do not work. It is that they are frequently used to answer a question they were never designed to address.

The pattern across all three is the same. The interventions that work best are the ones that stop heat being absorbed, rather than the ones that deal with it afterwards. Next week we will look at how these measures are costed, and why the cheapest of them is so often the last to be funded.
